strengths: The paper provides a carefully controlled, fully specified synthetic testbed (1D images, CLIP-style contrastive training) that cleanly isolates left-right relational learning from confounds present in web-scale VLMs; the dataset splits, generalization metrics, and training details are described with enough precision to reproduce the setup.

The mechanistic analysis is methodical and multi-pronged: head-level attention visualizations (Fig. 4), a formal weight-bias and token-position decomposition of pre-softmax attention logits (Eqs. 1-2), systematic ablations of EP/PE/PP/BP/VP terms (Fig. 5, Apps. D-H), and the observation that label-set recognition survives when left-right discrimination is ablated (App. G) jointly support the claim that a positional-embedding-induced horizontal attention gradient drives left-right discrimination.

The theoretical analysis in App. I is a genuine value-add: the condition |Π| > |T| for consistent directional preference is simple but explanatory, and the extension to RoPE (identifying bias-induced gradient and learned subspace alignment mechanisms, with PCA/SVD verification) both strengthens the theory and shows the authors anticipated an obvious objection to their learnable-positional-embedding mechanism.

Honest scoping of limitations: the discussion explicitly acknowledges that the 1D setting leaves open whether the mechanism transfers to 2D/naturalistic models, that multi-head interactions and cross-layer propagation are not fully resolved (Apps. K, L), and the negative result for 1-layer text encoders (App. J) is reported transparently.
The empirical finding that label diversity, rather than layout diversity, drives unseen-pair generalization (Fig. 3, App. B) is a clear, quantified takeaway with practical implications.
weaknesses: External validity is the central weakness: all conclusions derive from a toy 1D setting with images of length 10, ~25 object categories, and tiny models (1-2 layers, 4 heads). The abstract and framing ('CLIP-style Vision-Language Models', 'mechanistic insight of when and how CLIP-style models acquire relational competence') overstate the reach of the results; no experiment touches even small-scale real CLIP models (e.g., CLIP on ARO-style probes) to show that the positional-attention-gradient mechanism exists outside the testbed.

Statistical rigor is thin: results appear to come from single training runs (or at most a few), with no error bars, seed variance, or repeated-run statistics. Given that several conclusions hinge on moderate accuracy differences and phase-transition-like dynamics (App. C), single-run evidence is insufficient. The weight-decay comparison in App. B shows noisy, non-monotonic accuracy curves that are not clearly consistent with the claim that weight decay 'enhances generalization'.

The evaluation protocol is coarse: retrieval accuracy over validation sets of only 5 images per label/pair, with accuracy computed against candidate texts rather than a more sensitive continuous measure; subtle partial relational encoding could be missed or mischaracterized.

The causal story is established by inference-time ablation of logit terms, but ablating trained-in terms during inference is a somewhat indirect causal test; training with the terms constrained (or counterfactual initialization) would be a stronger intervention. The claim that the EP term is 'essential' is thus supported but not maximally rigorously.

Several results are under-analyzed or left open in ways that weaken the contribution: the text-encoder mechanism with both left/right representations is explicitly 'unclear' (Sec. 7); the phase-boundary loss jump in App. C is 'unclear at present'; single-head models fail for unexplained reasons (App. K).

Presentation issues: numerous typos ('labal pairs', 'Propablity', 'Conribution', 'disntance', 'serveral', inconsistent subscripts in Fig. 8 caption, 'PP, PP terms' in Fig. 5/16/17 captions), dense multi-panel figures (Figs. 5, 12, 19) that are hard to parse, and no mention of released code, which hurts reproducibility of the exact experiments despite the setup being describable.

strengths: The 1D synthetic testbed is well-designed and fully controllable, with clearly defined generalization splits (single-object positional, seen-pair configuration, unseen-pair) illustrated transparently in App. A, which reduces the risk of train/test leakage and makes the claims falsifiable within the setting.

The mechanistic analysis is methodical: the weight-bias decomposition of pre-softmax logits (Eq. 1) and the token/positional four-term decomposition (Eq. 2) are clean, the EP-term gradient is shown on generalizing vs. non-generalizing models (App. F), and inference-time ablations (Fig. 5e, App. G/H) provide causal evidence that position-dependent attention terms are needed for left-right discrimination.

The RoPE extension (App. I) goes beyond the default setup, offers a simple theoretical condition (|Π| > |T|) for why positional asymmetry must dominate token-dependent variation for OOD generalization, and empirically verifies two plausible mechanisms (bias-induced gradient and low-rank subspace alignment) with PCA/SVD evidence.
Hyperparameters, dataset sizes, and training details are documented, and the appendix covers architectural variations (heads, layers, weight decay) rather than cherry-picking a single configuration.
weaknesses: External validity is the central weakness: the entire mechanism is established only in a 1D, two-object, single-relation toy setting with tiny models. No experiment on real 2D CLIP/VLM checkpoints is offered to show that the positional-embedding attention-gradient mechanism actually explains (or even correlates with) spatial-reasoning behavior at scale. The discussion acknowledges this, but it substantially limits the significance of the contribution for the intended audience.

Statistical rigor is thin. Figures 3, 4(a), 8, 10, and 21 appear to be single training runs; accuracy curves are noisy and non-monotonic (e.g., Fig. 10 shows erratic behavior across weight-decay settings), yet claims such as 'label diversity, more than layout diversity, is the primary driver of generalization' rest on these unreplicated sweeps. No seeds, error bars, or confidence intervals are reported, and no code release is mentioned, hurting reproducibility.

The headline empirical finding is arguably predictable: that learnable positional embeddings interacting with token embeddings break left-right symmetry is close to what one would expect by construction, since positional embeddings are the only symmetry-breaking input. The paper does not compare against a plausible baseline (e.g., a model where symmetry is broken by other means) to establish that this specific EP-term gradient, rather than any asymmetric signal, is the operative mechanism.

The text-encoder side of the story is underdeveloped: Sec. 7/App. J show the 1-layer text encoder fails with paired left/right captions and a 2-layer fix 'works,' but the authors state the discrimination mechanism 'remains unclear due to the complexity in interpreting 2-layer Transformer model,' leaving half of the cross-modal alignment claim unexplained. The rotation-alignment result in Sec. 6.2 is also largely descriptive.

Presentation quality issues undermine confidence: multiple typos ('labal', 'Conribution to logit', 'serveral heads', 'propsoed'), a garbled hyperparameter description in the Fig. 8 caption (M_txt^B = 2, M_vis^rep = 1 listed oddly), a figure caption in Fig. 5(e) listing 'EP, PP, PP terms' (PP twice, BP missing), and dense multi-panel figures that are hard to parse (Figs. 5, 12, 14, 19).

Some conclusions overreach relative to evidence, e.g., attributing the loss jump near the phase boundary to grokking-like regularization effects (Sec. 3) on the basis of a single observation, and the claim that the EP term is 'essential' rests on inference-time zeroing that also removes other position-dependent information (partially disentangled only in App. H).

strengths: Well-designed, fully controlled synthetic testbed: the 1D image-text dataset cleanly isolates left-right relational understanding, and the three generalization types (single-object positional, seen-pair configuration, unseen-pair) are precisely defined with no train/test leakage (App. A).

The mechanistic account is unusually thorough for a toy study: pre-softmax attention logit decomposition into weight/bias and token/positional components (Eqs. 1-2), identification of the EP cross-term gradient, supporting statistics (Figs. 4c, 5c-d), causal ablation of the EP/PE/PP/BP terms (Fig. 5e), control analyses in non-generalizing models (App. F), and a value-path ablation (App. H) that together make the causal story fairly convincing within the toy setting.

The theoretical analysis (App. I) is a genuine strength: the consistency condition |Π| > |T| cleanly explains why position-dependent attention bias is necessary for unseen-pair generalization, and the RoPE extension identifies two concrete alternative mechanisms (bias-induced gradient, learned subspace alignment) that are validated empirically via PCA, SVD effective rank, and consistency-satisfaction rates (Fig. 19).

Complementary analyses (head pruning/retraining in App. K, 2-layer encoder in App. L, grokking-like phase dynamics in App. C, weight decay in App. B) show commendable breadth, and the paper is honest about what remains unexplained (e.g., loss jumps at phase boundaries, 2-layer text encoder interpretation).

The discussion candidly delineates scope: the authors explicitly state that whether the attention-gradient mechanism emerges in large-scale models on natural 2D images is open, which is the right framing for a controlled study.
weaknesses: External validity is the central weakness. The model operates on 1D images of length 10 with single-pixel objects and near-vocabulary-sized text; claims in the abstract/intro such as 'provide a mechanistic insight of when and how CLIP-style models acquire relational competence' overstate reach. Nothing in the paper demonstrates that the positional-embedding gradient mechanism operates in real CLIP/VLM encoders, so the practical significance for the spatial-reasoning problems motivating the introduction is unestablished.

The headline finding that 'label diversity, more than layout diversity, is the primary driver of generalization' may be partly definitional rather than a deep empirical discovery: unseen-pair generalization requires embedding generalization for held-out labels, so more training labels mechanically improves coverage of label-embedding structure. The paper does not fully disentangle this from a genuinely compositional learning effect.

Statistical rigor is weak: results appear to come from single training runs with no error bars or seed variation, and several key curves are noisy (Figs. 3, 10, 21). The claim that weight decay 'enhances generalization' (App. B) is poorly supported by the scattered curves in Fig. 10, and claims of phase structure in App. C are based on few trajectories.

Novelty is moderate. Attention-logit decomposition into query/key/bias and token/positional terms, and identifying position-embedding-driven attention biases, build on well-established mechanistic-interpretability toolkits; the contribution is applying these to a new (if simple) task rather than introducing new methodology, and related mechanistic work on spatial failures (e.g., Chen et al. 2025, Qi et al. 2025) is discussed but not directly compared experimentally.

In the both-left-and-right-caption setting (Sec. 7), the authors concede they cannot interpret how the text encoder discriminates XLY/XRY/YLX/YRX in the 2-layer model, leaving the alignment half of the story incomplete; similarly, multi-head interaction (App. K) and multi-layer propagation (App. L) are left open, so the 'mechanistic account' is complete only for the narrowest configuration.

Reproducibility support is thin: no code release is mentioned, and there are a number of typos and sloppiness ('labal', 'propsoed', 'disntance', 'serveral', 'Conribution', inconsistent label claims such as 'EP, PP, PP terms' in Fig. 5(e)/16/17 captions) that suggest the manuscript needed another careful pass.

strengths: Well-designed, controllable synthetic testbed (1D image-text pairs with one/two objects) that cleanly isolates left-right relational learning under a CLIP-style contrastive objective, with clearly defined generalization types (single-object positional, seen-pair configuration, unseen-pair) and careful dataset splits to avoid leakage (App. A).

The mechanistic analysis is thorough and well-supported within the toy setting: the weight-bias and token/positional decomposition of pre-softmax attention logits (Sec. 5, Apps. E-F) is interpretable, the horizontal EP-term gradient is shown in generalizing but not non-generalizing models (App. G), and inference-time ablations of the EP/PP/BP/VP terms causally tie the gradient to left-right discrimination (Fig. 5e, Apps. H, I, M).

The paper goes beyond the core setting with meaningful extensions: RoPE-based training with a two-mechanism theoretical account validated empirically (App. J), 2D images (App. K), 3-object scenes (App. N), an autoregressive VLM (App. O), and an approximate LayerNorm decomposition for non-linear models (App. R), which strengthen the plausibility that the mechanism is not an artifact of one narrow setup.

The finding that label diversity, rather than layout diversity, is the primary driver of generalization is a crisp, actionable empirical result, and the discussion connecting it to data-diversity/compositional-generalization work (Uselis et al., 2025) is thoughtful.

Honest limitations discussion: the authors clearly acknowledge the gap to large-scale VLMs on natural images, the open questions about multi-head interactions and cross-layer propagation, and the preliminary nature of the LayerNorm analysis.
weaknesses: Limited external validity: all central claims are established in a deliberately simplified setting with D_image=10, ~20 discrete object categories, single-pixel objects, and a 1-layer attention-only encoder for the main mechanistic results. The authors themselves note that bridging to natural images and large-scale VLMs remains open; the paper's significance therefore rests on the hope (not demonstration) that the mechanism generalizes, following the toy-model tradition.

No evidence of statistical robustness: results appear to come from single training runs per configuration (no seeds, error bars, or repeated trials reported), despite visibly noisy accuracy curves (e.g., Fig. 10 weight-decay results are erratic; several generalization curves are non-monotonic). Claims like 'label diversity is the primary driver' would be more convincing with run-to-run variance quantified.

Some empirical results are noisy or incompletely explained: weight-decay effects (App. C) are difficult to interpret from the plots; the phase-boundary loss-jump asymmetry in App. D is explicitly left unexplained; the text-encoder analysis in the bidirectional setting (Sec. 7) concedes that how the model discriminates among XLY/XRY/YLX/YRX 'remains unclear'.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: hyperparameters and compute are documented and the implementation builds on public codebases, but there is no stated commitment to releasing the authors' own code/data, which would be particularly valuable for a paper whose contribution is a testbed.

Presentation issues: several typos and figure/caption problems (e.g., 'labal', 'propsoed', 'Consribution', inconsistent 'd_txt^rep' notation in Fig. 8 caption, Fig. 5(d) legend repeating the same inequality for both categories), and the main-text figure density (Figs. 4-5) makes the core mechanistic argument harder to follow than it needs to be.

The theoretical condition |Π| > |T| (App. J) is a reasonable but fairly simple argument; its necessity claim ('position-dependent asymmetry is necessary') holds only under the assumed 1-layer, linear-attention decomposition and is not tested against alternative mechanisms in a falsifiable way.

strengths: A genuinely controlled and well-designed synthetic testbed: the 1D/2D image-text task with disjoint train/test label splits cleanly isolates relational generalization from recognition, and the three generalization types (single-object positional, seen-pair configuration, unseen-pair) are carefully defined with an explicit no-leak schematic (Fig. 9).

The mechanistic account is unusually complete for a toy setting: attention-logit decomposition (Eq. 1-2), causal inference-time ablations of the EP/PP/BP terms (Fig. 5e, App. M), a non-generalizing control model showing the gradient is absent (App. G), and a simple theory (App. J) deriving the consistency condition |Π| > |T| that ties positional asymmetry to unseen-pair generalization.

Good breadth of validation within the toy scope: the mechanism is checked under left-only vs. bidirectional captions (Sec. 7, App. L/M), 2D images (App. K), 3-object scenes (App. N), an autoregressive VLM (App. O), RoPE position encodings with two distinct mechanisms (App. J.3), and an approximate LayerNorm decomposition for non-linear models (App. R).

The paper is honest about scope: the discussion clearly delineates what remains open (bridging to natural images, deeper layers, head interactions) rather than overclaiming transfer to real CLIP models.
weaknesses: External validity is the central concern: the entire mechanistic story rests on a 1-layer, 4-head, attention-only transformer over 1D discrete token images with hand-crafted single-token relation words. Nothing in the paper demonstrates that the EP-term gradient is a plausible account of spatial reasoning in actual CLIP-style models; the 2D and 3-object extensions remain in the same toy family. For an ICML main-track paper claiming insight into 'how CLIP-style models acquire relational competence,' the gap between the testbed and the claimed target system is large and only acknowledged, not bridged.

No evidence of statistical robustness: the results appear to be single training runs per configuration. Curves in Fig. 3 and especially the weight-decay sweeps in Fig. 10 are visibly noisy and non-monotonic, yet the headline claim that 'label diversity, more than layout diversity, is the primary driver of generalization' is made without seeds, error bars, or any quantitative significance analysis. This is a serious evidential gap for the paper's second main contribution.

The mechanistic analysis is performed on a simplified architecture (no LayerNorm/MLP) that the authors show behaves 'qualitatively similarly,' but causality of the EP term in the full model is only addressed via a preliminary approximate LayerNorm decomposition (App. R) applied to the first layer only. The claim that the gradient is 'essential' is strictly established only for the reduced model.

The 'label diversity vs. layout diversity' finding is coarse: both are varied only through N_pair/n_2 proxies, and confounds (e.g., total data volume, batch composition) are not disentangled, making the causal interpretation of 'label diversity is the primary driver' weakly supported relative to how prominently it is claimed in the abstract.

Some analyses are under-specified or presented selectively: the rotation-based image-text embedding alignment (Sec. 6.2) is an intriguing observation but the 'rotation' hypothesis is fitted post hoc with no theoretical justification; Fig. 5(d) legend conditions in the caption appear garbled/identical; several claims (e.g., text encoder capacity explanation in Sec. 7) rest on a single architecture contrast.

No statement of code release despite the work being heavily reproducibility-dependent; only the underlying public codebases are listed (App. B.2). Given that conclusions hinge on exact decomposition and ablation procedures, this limits reproducibility.

Writing is dense and the paper buries its main quantitative claims in figures; the relation between the abstract's strong framing ('mechanistic insight of when and how CLIP-style models acquire relational competence') and what is actually established (a mechanism in a 1-layer toy model) is overstated.

strengths: Well-controlled, clearly described synthetic testbed (1D image-text pairs with a CLIP-style contrastive objective) that cleanly isolates left-right relational learning from confounds present in natural image-text data.

The mechanistic claim is supported by multiple converging lines of evidence: attention pattern analysis (Fig. 4), an interpretable decomposition of pre-softmax logits into EE/EP/PE/PP terms (Fig. 5), qualitative comparison with non-generalizing models (App. G), and inference-time ablation showing EP-term removal drops left-right discrimination to chance while preserving object-set recognition (App. H).

The theoretical analysis in App. J is a genuine strength: the consistency condition |Π| > |T| gives a crisp rationale for why a position-dependent attention bias is necessary for OOD generalization to unseen object pairs, and the RoPE extension (bias-induced gradient vs. learned subspace alignment, verified via PCA/SVD of W_K) is thorough.

Good breadth of robustness checks: bidirectional text representations (Sec. 7, App. L, M), 2D images (App. K), 3-object scenes (App. N), autoregressive VLMs (App. O), head-count analysis (App. P), and an approximate LayerNorm decomposition for nonlinear models (App. R).

The limitations discussion is honest and appropriately scoped: the authors explicitly state the setting is deliberately simplified, that bridging to natural images and large-scale VLMs remains open, and they do not overclaim.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: full hyperparameter details, dataset construction schematics (App. A), and compute accounting (App. B).
weaknesses: External validity is the central limitation. The mechanism is established in 1-layer, attention-only transformers over 10-token discrete sequences; the paper itself cannot demonstrate that positional-embedding attention gradients are responsible for spatial competence in real CLIP-style models. The one-page 2D extension (4x4 flattened tokens) and the approximate LayerNorm analysis mitigate this only partially, so the significance rests largely on the 'toy models have historically generalized' argument.

Statistical rigor is thin. Results appear to come from single training runs with no seeds, error bars, or variance reporting; several curves (e.g., Fig. 3, Fig. 10, App. C weight-decay study) are visibly noisy and non-monotonic, which weakens the claim that 'label diversity is the primary driver of generalization' and that weight decay systematically helps. These are core empirical claims and should be supported by repeats.

The dataset scale is very small (N_tot up to ~25 object categories, n1=n2=5-20 images per label). With so few distinct labels, it is unclear how robust the label-vs-layout diversity finding is, and how sensitive the mechanism is to dataset size, positions (D_image=10 gives only 45 two-object configurations), and hyperparameters.

No explicit code release is promised. Given that the paper's value is as a testbed and methodology for others, and that implementation builds on modified third-party codebases, releasing code/data would substantially strengthen reproducibility.

Presentation could be improved: Figures 4-5 and 20-22 are dense heatmaps that are hard to parse; the main-text narrative sometimes defers key evidence entirely to appendices (e.g., App. J theory, App. M bidirectional ablations), and there are typos ('labal', 'is enhanced' grammar, inconsistent 'Disntangling').

The contribution is necessarily incremental relative to the mechanistic interpretability canon (it applies established logit-decomposition and ablation methodology from Transformer Circuits to a new VLM task), so its impact depends on whether the identified mechanism proves general - which the paper can only argue, not show.
